subtype: Stage 7: Guilt, relief and mixed feelings [Actor]
passage:
Dear Mridul,
It's been five weeks since Papa died, and I haven't told anyone this.
For two years I slept on the folding cot beside his bed at home. I woke for every cough and learned the beeps of his oxygen machine better than my own phone.
The morning after the funeral, I slept nine hours straight. I woke up and felt light. Relieved. And then I felt sick about feeling it.
What kind of son is glad his father is gone?
But I'm not glad he's gone. I miss his terrible jokes, the way he said, "Eshu, come, sit." I cry in the shower most days.
Both are true, and I've been hiding the relief like it's something dirty. Writing it to you is the first time it has felt a little lighter.
You sat with him on Sundays so I could rest. Maybe you understand.
Eshaan

qa.q: How long did Eshaan sleep the morning after the funeral?
qa.a: He slept nine hours straight.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan feel sick after feeling relieved?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, as if a good son shouldn't feel light after his father's death, even though he misses Papa and cries most days.

qa.q: What turning point does writing this letter open for Eshaan?
qa.a: Saying the relief to someone who knew Papa lets the shame lose some weight; talking more with Mridul, or later with a grief counsellor, can keep it from staying hidden.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Mridul, who sat with Papa on Sundays, may feel trusted and moved, and may even recognise some of the same mixed feelings about the long illness ending.

grounding: Shows a caregiver feeling relief after a long illness ends, then shame about that relief, and the first step of not hiding it.

subtype: Stage 7: Guilt, relief and mixed feelings [Actor]
passage:
You want the honest version, Rafiq? Okay.
When Dadi died in March, after three years of forgetting my name, my Bua hugged me at the cremation and said, "Jahnavi, you were such a good granddaughter." And all I could think was, I get my evenings back. I can take the Bengaluru job.
Then I went home and couldn't eat. Because what kind of person thinks that at her Dadi's pyre?
I haven't said this to anyone. Not Papa. Not even my therapist.
I do miss her. I miss her humming while she oiled my hair, back when she still knew me. But I also miss sleeping. Both feel true, and I keep swallowing one of them.
...You're not looking at me like I'm a monster.
Huh. That actually helps.

qa.q: What did Bua say to Jahnavi at the cremation?
qa.a: "Jahnavi, you were such a good granddaughter."

qa.q: Why couldn't Jahnavi eat after going home?
qa.a: She was ashamed of feeling relieved about getting her evenings back, and wondered what kind of person thinks that at her Dadi's pyre.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do next with the feeling she has been swallowing?
qa.a: She could bring it to her therapist the way she just did with Rafiq, since saying it aloud already made it lighter.

qa.q: What is it like for Rafiq to hear this?
qa.a: Rafiq is trusted with something Jahnavi has told no one, and Rafiq's calm, non-judging face shows her the relief can be spoken without losing a friend.

grounding: Illustrates grief and relief existing together after years of caregiving, and how hiding the shame keeps it heavy.

subtype: Stage 7: Guilt, relief and mixed feelings [Actor]
passage:
Diary, two weeks after
Amma died on the 3rd. Two years of hospital visits, night feeds, oxygen cylinders. Two years of me sleeping on the floor beside her bed.
And the thing I can't tell anyone: the first morning after, I slept until nine. I woke up and there was no alarm, no medicine chart, and for one second I felt light. Relieved.
Then I felt sick. What kind of daughter feels relieved?
Deepika came over today. I almost told her. I said, "I miss her so much," which is true. I didn't say the other thing, which is also true.
Maybe next time.
Leela

qa.q: How long had Leela cared for Amma?
qa.a: Two years.

qa.q: What did Leela feel on the first morning after, and then what?
qa.a: Leela felt a moment of relief, then sick with shame for feeling it.

qa.q: What small step could lighten Leela's shame?
qa.a: Telling Deepika or a counsellor about the relief, since saying it aloud can show it is common and not a betrayal.

qa.q: How might Deepika see Leela during the visit?
qa.a: Deepika probably sees a grieving daughter who misses her mother, without knowing about the hidden shame.

grounding: Shows a caregiver who, after her mother's long illness and death, feels relief alongside grief and then shame she keeps hidden.

passage:
Sunaina: can I tell you something awful
Hemant: nothing you say is awful. go on
Sunaina: since Papa died, part of me is relieved. no more nights in the ICU. no more watching him in pain
Sunaina: and I hate myself for it
Hemant: Sunaina. you looked after him for three years
Sunaina: that's not an excuse
Hemant: it's not an excuse, it's the reason. you can miss him and be relieved it's over. both can be true
Sunaina: really?
Hemant: really. the counsellor told me the same after Dadi. it's common
Sunaina: I've been scared to say it to anyone
Hemant: you just did. call you in 10?

qa.a: Three years.

qa.a: Sunaina feels ashamed and guilty about her relief, as if it betrays her grief for Papa.

qa.q: What turning point does Hemant offer?
qa.a: Hemant says both feelings can be true and are common, and offers to call, which helps Sunaina stop hiding the shame.

qa.q: What might Hemant be feeling when he says "you just did"?
qa.a: Hemant seems warm and proud of Sunaina for speaking up, wanting to offer support right away.

grounding: Shows a caregiver admitting relief after her father's long illness and death, her shame, and a friend telling her both feelings can be true.

subtype: Stage 7: Guilt, relief and mixed feelings [Actor]
passage:
In the small town of Mapusa, the house was quiet again after the funeral crowds left. Shalini sat on the verandah where she'd pushed Avó's wheelchair every evening for four years.
Francis from next door came with a pot of tea, as he had every day of the illness.
"How are you really?" he asked.
Shalini looked at the empty wheelchair. "Honestly? I slept a full night for the first time in four years. And I felt... lighter. And now I feel terrible for feeling lighter."
Francis nodded slowly. "My mother said the same after my father. It doesn't mean you didn't love her."
Shalini's shoulders dropped. She reached for the tea and cried, properly, for the first time.

qa.q: How long had Shalini pushed Avó's wheelchair?
qa.a: Four years.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she said she felt terrible?
qa.a: Shalini felt ashamed and guilty about feeling lighter, alongside her grief for Avó.

qa.q: What did Francis do that helped?
qa.a: He asked how she really was and told her his mother felt the same, showing her relief doesn't mean she didn't love Avó.

qa.q: What is it like for Francis to hear Shalini's confession?
qa.a: Francis seems calm and understanding, remembering his own family's grief and wanting to lift her shame.

grounding: Shows a caregiver confessing relief after her grandmother's long illness and death, then shame, and finding it lighter once spoken.

subtype: Stage 7: Guilt, relief and mixed feelings [Actor]
passage: The first morning after the funeral, Rosa woke at nine. For two years she had woken at three, then five, listening for her father's cough through the wall of the terraced house in Manchester. Now there was only the rain and a car door somewhere down the street. She lay still and felt something loosen in her chest: relief. A heartbeat later came a hot wave of shame. What kind of daughter feels relieved? She told no one for a week. When Chidi from next door brought soup and asked how she was sleeping, Rosa blurted, "Too well. I hate myself for it." Chidi sat down at the kitchen table. "You loved him, and you were exhausted. My mum said the same after my gran. Both things are true." Rosa cried then, properly, for the first time since the hospital.

qa.q: At what times did Rosa used to wake during the two years of caring?
qa.a: She woke at three, then five, listening for her father's cough.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Rosa have that first morning?
qa.a: She felt relief loosening her chest, then a hot wave of shame about feeling relieved at all.

qa.q: What helped Rosa's shame start to lift?
qa.a: Saying it out loud to Chidi, who answered that love and exhaustion can both be true, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How does Chidi seem to see Rosa's relief?
qa.a: Chidi sees it as normal, not shameful, having heard Chidi's own mum say the same after a gran died.

grounding: Shows a caregiver feeling relief alongside grief after a long illness ends in death, then shame about the relief until it is spoken aloud.
